source_description: Arthur O. Lovejoy notebook labelled ‘Sankhya + Buddhism’

batch.method: Manual visual correction against rendered PDF pages, using PaddleOCR-VL only as a scaffold.
batch.policy: Preserve readable Lovejoy terminology and abbreviations; normalize obvious OCR errors; mark difficult handwriting and technical forms rather than silently reconstructing them.
batch.status: first pass complete; direct-image material/text verification propagated for pp.41-54; p.48 substantive correction and Round-17b p.42/p.49-52 relation-wording controls merged from original split-PDF witness

research_signals_from_batch: The notebook turns from dependent origination to the five khandhas as an overlapping classificatory system.

PDF pp.41-42 visually map correspondences among nāmarūpa, rūpa, vedanā, saññā, saṅkhāra and viññāṇa; p.42 is image-secure for the contrast between spatial/classificatory inclusion and temporal antecedence.
The saṅkhāras are treated as a heterogeneous psychological catalogue; the Milindapañha soul/window analogy is used against a substantial self.
Upādāna/upadhi become a philological and structural problem: clinging, substratum/support, and collective designation are compared.
The notebook tests whether a composite nidāna chain remains logically intelligible rather than merely accidental; p.49 directly states that a discoverable logical system governs the arrangement.
Avijjā and saṅkhāra are traced toward Upanishadic and Sāṁkhya-Yoga conceptual backgrounds while historical origin is kept distinct from logical arrangement and scholastic reconciliation.
The final pages connect upādāna/upadhi, karma, rebirth and āsava terminology through etymological notes on support, clinging and flowing.

pages.corrected_text: Infinity of Causal Series. MP II. 32, 3: Nagasena says the ‘ultimate point of time is not apparent’ and illustrates this with a recurring natural series and an abridged dependent-origination sequence: eye/form → sight → contact → sensation (vedana) → desire (tanha) → karma → renewed production of the eye. Nagasena further explains that the ultimate point of separate links may be known, but not that of the whole series. [Lower passage partly illegible.]
uncertain_readings: some words in quoted causal sequence

pages.corrected_text: [Short continuation at top only; mostly illegible.] ‘absolute first destruction … time totally’ [?].

Form. Rupam. v. Warren p. 487. Derivative forms are described as forms springing or proceeding from the four great elements. Lovejoy lists the four physical sense-organs (ayatanas) and the sensible qualities connected with them: form for the eye, sound for the ear, odor for the nose, taste for the tongue, and bodily qualities for the body. Final paragraph notes the intelligibility, despite awkwardness, of this reduction/classification.

The Khandhas = form, sensation, perception, dispositions/conformations, consciousness. [Facing-page notes cite Majjhima Nikaya and use the removal-of-fuel / cessation-of-fire analogy; exact wording remains partly uncertain.]
uncertain_readings: several small labels in the larger cross-system map

pages.corrected_text: Khandhas. Vedana. Vedana is treated both as a subdivision of nama and as a link in the causal chain. Lovejoy notes a double threefold classification yielding eighteen sorts: by affective quality (pleasant, unpleasant, indifferent) and by sensory source (eye, ear, etc.), so the sensation from each organ may have any of the three affective qualities.
uncertain_readings: one phrase describing the two threefold divisions

pages.corrected_text: Khandhas. Vinnana. For evidence of the primacy of vinnana, Lovejoy notes that the four mental khandhas are collectively termed a ‘conscious group’ and points again to vinnana’s place in paticca-samuppada. A Rhys Davids note treats consciousness as extensively subdivided for Buddhist psychology, culminating in a classification into 89 classes.

Khandhas. Sanna. Childers/Rhys Davids: ideas are divided into six classes corresponding to the six classes of sensation; e.g. blue/tree under sight, sweetness under taste. The Sankhara: ‘52 divisions not mutually exclusive.’ Lovejoy begins a long list including contact (phassa), sensation (vedana), idea/perception (sanna), reflection (manasikara), memory (sati), vitality (jivitindriya), attention (vitakka), investigation (vicara), effort (viriya), joy (piti), and many later moral/mental qualities; numerous Pali glosses in the list remain uncertain.
uncertain_readings: many Pali glosses and English equivalents in the 52-item list

pages.corrected_text: The Sankhara. In later Buddhist psychology they are divided into 52 divisions, practically encompassing the human mental qualities/capabilities that make up the individual; Lovejoy remarks on the miscellaneous and repetitive character of the list. Attan: Milindapanha II.3.6 asks whether nama/soul is a living principle within the body. The king compares the soul using the senses to someone looking from different windows of a palace. Nagasena replies by reductio: if one inner soul used the organs indiscriminately, it should be able to see by the ear, etc., which it cannot.

Upadana. Oldenberg treats upadana and upadhi as almost synonymous. Nirvana is made dependent on non-presence of upadhi nearly as much as on upadana. A Samyutta Nikaya causal series runs from tanha to upadhi and thence to old age/death; paticca-samuppada analogously runs tanha → upadana → later links. Upadhi is glossed as laying one thing on another / giving it support; upadana as substratum and also laying hold of, clinging to, as a flame catches fuel. Fuel or that which is laid hold of can itself be called upadana.

Continuation on upadana/upadhi. Clinging and the act of clinging are both associated with upadana; despite different derivations, upadana and upadhi acquire overlapping senses of support/substratum/clinging. A Pali quotation from Samyutta Nikaya is retained as uncertain. In a Senart note on the twelve nidanas, Lovejoy asks whether upadana is only an abbreviation for upadana-skandhas, or more exactly the five skandhas collectively. He then observes that at least three of the skandhas, although included collectively under upadana, appear separately in nidanas 2 (sankhara), 3 (vinnana), and 7 (vedana); rupa, a fourth, is at least directly recalled by namarupa (4), while the fifth, sanna, is represented through two terms whose exact wording remains uncertain. The page is therefore testing duplication produced by a collective designation, not enumerating doctrinal forms of upadana.
uncertain_readings: exact final phrase for how sanna is represented
pages.editorial_argument_summary: Original-image recheck corrects the prior first-pass summary: the page concerns recurrence of skandha constituents under a collective upadana designation, not a list of distinct doctrinal forms of upadana.

pages.corrected_text: Upadana / nidana formula continued. Lovejoy grants that the terms of the formula are not original to Buddhism and are brought together from pre-existing sources; objective and subjective elements are mingled, and the sequence is not homogeneous. The immediately following qualifier is crossed/overwritten and is not frozen diplomatically. He then rejects Senart's stronger conclusion: the formula is not simply ‘illogical & unintelligible’ and its terms have not merely been ‘jumbled together in an order more or less accidental.’ Lovejoy writes that ‘There is a discoverable logical system wh. governs the arrangement, and the repetitions are intentional; as I hope I have succeeded in showing.’
pages.transcription_confidence: high for key conclusion; medium for preceding crossed clause
uncertain_readings: crossed/overwritten qualifier after not homogeneous / strictly

pages.editorial_argument_summary: Composite provenance and imperfect homogeneity are kept distinct from logical intelligibility. The manuscript says logical system, not technical system.

pages.corrected_text: The duplication problem continues. Lovejoy argues that one would otherwise have not merely a double but a triple enumeration of the khandhas; namarupa itself is also a collective designation, while related constituents can recur separately. The lower passage directly states that terms can ‘precede both temporally as well as logically.’ Several compressed numbered technical labels remain unresolved.
pages.transcription_confidence: medium-high for argument anchors; low-medium for compressed list
pages.diplomatic_visible_text: For we should then have not merely a double but a triple enumeration of F. khandhas ... Namarupa itself, we know, is also a collective designation ... precede both temporally as well as logically ...

pages.corrected_text: Nidanas. Senart p. 285: the enumeration might easily be abridged or extended; Lovejoy then turns to whether avijja and sankhara belong to Buddhism ab initio and to the historical/genealogical status of those opening terms. A key right-leaf passage says that a practical and natural interpretation would not by itself justify the ontological function assigning avijja its place at the head of the nidanas. Lovejoy immediately asks, ‘But is tre necessarily any ontological function involved? A.O.L.’ Sankhara's position is then connected with an outside tradition, probably Samkhya-Yoga; exact compressed technical wording remains partly uncertain.
pages.transcription_confidence: high for source/ontological anchors; medium for compressed genealogy details
uncertain_readings: alternate-series citation and several Pali terms
exact Samkhya-Yoga wording below the A.O.L. question

That is an interpretation very practical & natural; but it wld never have justified the ontological function wh. gives to avijjā F. place it occupied at F. head of F. nidānas. But is tre necessarily any ontological function involved? A.O.L.
pages.material_layout_observation: The spread is densely written across both leaves. The initials A.O.L. sit immediately after the ontological-function question inside the source/analysis run, creating an unusually explicit material seam between source digest and a marked Lovejoy intervention.
pages.witness_status: W3 for heading, Senart anchor, practical/ontological contrast and A.O.L. question; W1-W2 for compressed Pali series
pages.editorial_argument_summary: This page shifts from logical arrangement toward historical genealogy, while the A.O.L.-marked question records Lovejoy's own local challenge to an ontological reading.

pages.corrected_text: Continuation: sankharas persist through successive existences as germs/conditions of future existence. The image-secure conclusion states that ‘the whole enumeration is secondary as to origin & composite as to character.’ Lovejoy then asks ‘And what of namarupa?’ and tests a scholastic reconciliation of rupa/nama with the skandhas. On the right leaf he calls one such reconciliation ‘plainly only a scholastic expedient, without warrant’ and closes by resisting the authority of a theory ‘conceived all of a piece.’ Exact compressed Sanskrit/Pali connective clauses remain partly uncertain.

pages.editorial_argument_summary: Historical origin, logical arrangement, and scholastic reconciliation are treated as different questions. Composite origin does not by itself imply accidental arrangement or whole-system borrowing.

pages.corrected_text: Upadana/upadhi are repeatedly treated as causes of differences in rebirth. The khandhas cannot simply be destroyed by an individual moral act; karma does not die at once but waits until the combination of khandhas to which previous karma gave rise naturally dissolves. Right-page notes revisit the etymology of upadhi/upadana: support/substratum versus clinging/finding support. Lovejoy then turns to the asavas and lists four forms, with active/passive senses and related compounds; exact Pali forms are partly uncertain.

Asava / etymology continued. From a Majjhima Nikaya passage involving Buddhist etymological wordplay, Lovejoy considers whether the technical term should be recognized through a verbal sense connected with ‘flowing’ / ‘flowing away.’ He prefers the verbal derivation and argues that the transition from an ordinary meaning of flowing to a technical meaning such as ‘impurity’ is otherwise gratuitous. Exact Pali quotation and section reference remain uncertain.
